tldr: This survey organizes rapidly growing surgical video generation research (2024–2026), tracking the technological shift from synthesizing visual realism to capturing causal dynamics and physical laws via world models, along with future challenges.
hero_caption: The transition across three paradigms in surgical video generation: evolving from (a) unconditional generation that synthesizes visually plausible videos from noise, to (b) conditional generation controlled by prompts such as text or masks, and finally to (c) world modeling generation that resolves state transitions and causal dynamics driven by robot actions.
overview:
Training models for surgical robotic autonomy and intraoperative perception requires massive amounts of surgical video data. However, real-world clinical environments face three major bottlenecks: strict patient privacy regulations, a scarcity of data for rare cases or intraoperative complications, and prohibitive annotation costs. Synthetic surgical video generation powered by generative AI has emerged as a promising breakthrough to address this severe data scarcity.

With advancements in video diffusion models, surgical video generation research exploded between 2024 and 2026. Until now, however, the field lacked a unified conceptual framework. The authors organize recent literature into three paradigms based on generative purpose: unconditional generation that reproduces realistic appearances from noise, conditional generation that steers outputs using text or trajectories, and world modeling generation that models physical and causal scene changes in response to robot actions.

A cross-sectional review of public datasets and benchmark experiments reveals a persistent gap between pixel-level fidelity and clinical plausibility: models often achieve high scores on standard image and video metrics (such as FVD and SSIM) while producing anatomical breakdowns and physically impossible tissue deformations. To enable applications in surgical simulation and robotic policy learning, moving beyond statistical visual replication toward world models that integrate biophysics and state transitions is crucially important.
contributions: Structured the 2024–2026 surgical video generation literature for the first time into three paradigms: unconditional generation, conditional generation, and world modeling generation.
Formulated the surgical video generation task, highlighting the technical shift from appearance imitation to action-driven state transition models.
Summarized major public datasets and quantitative benchmark results of representative methods to provide objective comparative references.
Identified the gap between pixel-level fidelity and clinical plausibility, outlining open challenges and future directions in generalization, physical realism, and reliability.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need to Generate Surgical Videos Now?
sections.summary: Developing surgical AI and autonomous robots requires vast amounts of video, but privacy constraints and scarce rare cases hinder real-world progress. This section explains why synthetic video generation matters and why a dedicated survey is needed.
sections.details:
Research applying robotics and AI to surgery is accelerating worldwide, but high-quality intraoperative video is essential for training these models. Clinical data collection faces three formidable hurdles: data sharing restrictions due to patient privacy regulations, a long-tail distribution with very few instances of rare complications, and enormous annotation costs for labeling surgical tools and tool-tissue interactions.

Generative AI has garnered significant attention as a way to bypass these bottlenecks. With the rise of video diffusion models and large vision-language models (VLMs), synthesizing clinically meaningful videos has become feasible. However, surgical video generation differs fundamentally from general domain video synthesis. It strictly demands anatomical topological accuracy (correct organ relationships), standard surgical procedural logic, and physical plausibility when instruments contact living tissue. Merely looking visually plausible is not enough for medical deployment.

Although related studies surged between 2024 and 2026, individual methods remained fragmented without an overarching conceptual map. Prior biomedical generation surveys largely categorized methods by modality, such as MRI or endoscopy. In contrast, this survey focuses exclusively on surgical video generation, unpacking how the core purpose of generation has evolved.

sections.heading: Formulating Surgical Video Generation with Math
sections.summary: We formulate surgical video generation as learning a conditional probability distribution. The intended nature of the model changes significantly depending on whether the conditioning signal specifies appearance or represents an action driving state transitions.
sections.details:
Let a surgical video be a sequence of $T$ frames, $V = \{v_1, \ldots, v_T\}$. The goal of surgical video generation is to learn the conditional probability distribution $p(V \mid C)$ given a conditioning signal $C$. What goes into $C$—or whether it is empty—defines the nature of the problem.

In unconditional generation, $C$ is empty, and the model learns the data distribution $p(V)$ across the dataset directly. In conditional generation, $C$ represents appearance or semantic cues indicating what the video should depict, such as text prompts, instrument segmentation masks, or surgical phase labels.

World modeling generation takes this a step further. Here, $C$ represents an "action" performed by a robot or surgeon. Rather than simply rendering a specified appearance, the model aims to capture causal dynamics: predicting how the surgical scene evolves over time when an intervention (action) is applied to the current state.

sections.heading: Three Paradigms: From Diffusion to World Models
sections.summary: The literature is categorized into unconditional generation, conditional generation, and world modeling generation. The technological focus is clearly shifting from visual realism to modeling causal relationships and physical laws.
sections.details:
The authors organize surgical video generation research into three paradigms based on the generative purpose:

- **III-A Unconditional Generation**
This approach synthesizes realistic surgical videos directly from random noise without external prompts. A prominent example, Endora, adopted Diffusion Transformers (DiT) for endoscopic simulation, demonstrating for the first time that diffusion models can learn the unconditional distribution of surgical videos. It was a critical step proving the feasibility of reproducing complex surgical scene textures using diffusion models.

- **III-B Conditional Generation**
Once unconditional synthesis became viable, the demand arose to generate specific surgical scenes on demand. This led to conditional generation. An early pioneer, VISAGE, performed future frame prediction from an initial frame and an action triplet (instrument, verb, target). Control capabilities expanded rapidly with interactive frameworks offering text- and mask-guided editing, MS-PCD accounting for phase progression, SurgSora enabling trajectory control without segmentation masks, and HieraSurg synthesizing fine details from coarse semantic shifts hierarchically. Diverse conditioning signals have been introduced: Ophora based on the large-scale cataract dataset Ophora-160K, LLaMA-VG leveraging VLMs, SG2VID using scene graphs, MoViS capturing instrument kinematics via keypoints, and Blob incorporating 3D spatial awareness.

- **III-C World Modeling Generation**
Conditional generation merely learns correlations; it does not understand how a scene causally responds to actions. To bridge this, world models explicitly model the environment's state transition probability $p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)$. A representative method, SWoMo, employs a hybrid architecture: symbolic components combining a rule-based physics engine with physical scene graphs handle tissue deformation and causal relations, while a diffusion model renders visually realistic frames.

- **III-D Summary**
The overall trajectory clearly shifts from synthesizing plausible frames to achieving controllability, and finally to acquiring causal dynamics to support robotic decision-making.

sections.heading: Current Benchmarks: Visually Pleasing, but Clinically Plausible?
sections.summary: We review the public datasets, common evaluation metrics, and experimental results underpinning surgical video generation. High scores on standard image metrics do not guarantee real clinical utility.
sections.details:
Public datasets and objective evaluation are vital to advancing surgical video generation. This section reviews the current landscape:

- **IV-A Public Datasets**
Major datasets centered on laparoscopic surgery (such as Cholec80) and robot-assisted surgery (such as JIGSAWS) drive current research. However, most remain limited to specific procedures or single institutions, and their scale is very small compared to datasets used in general video generation.

- **IV-B Evaluation Metrics and Quantitative Results**
The paper compiles reported values across representative methods. Common metrics include FVD (Fréchet Video Distance) for overall video quality, FID for frame-level fidelity, SSIM for structural similarity, as well as PSNR, LPIPS, and frame-to-frame consistency. Summarized benchmark tables confirm that generation quality has steadily improved across methods.

However, the authors issue a strong cautionary note: existing metrics like FVD and FID merely assess whether frames look like natural images or videos. In extreme cases, an organ might tear in an anatomically impossible direction or an instrument might clip through tissue; as long as the pixel textures look clear, FVD will still yield a favorable score. Because video durations and procedural difficulties vary, direct comparisons across datasets are difficult, highlighting an urgent need for medical-specific evaluation standards.

sections.heading: Three Core Hurdles and Promising Future Directions
sections.summary: We examine three fundamental challenges in current methods—data and generalization, physical realism and controllability, and evaluation and reliability—and suggest key research directions.
sections.details:
Several major barriers must be overcome before surgical video generation can be reliably deployed for simulation or robot reinforcement learning:

- **V-A Data and Generalization Hurdles**
Most existing models are trained on data from single centers or specific camera systems. Consequently, they are fragile against domain shifts caused by lighting changes, different camera models, and patient-specific anatomical variations. Adopting unsupervised domain adaptation from computer vision and large-scale pre-training via surgical foundation models (such as SurgVISTA) will be essential moving forward.

- **V-B Physical Realism and Controllability Hurdles**
Current diffusion models merely mimic visual patterns statistically from data; they do not solve for tissue deformation properties, tool contact forces, or fluid dynamics like bleeding. As a result, they frequently generate videos that violate physical laws. Future approaches must explicitly integrate biomechanical priors into generation architectures. In addition, intuitive control mechanisms beyond text or coarse trajectories are needed to guide complex surgical actions.

- **V-C Evaluation and Reliability Hurdles**
As noted, pixel-level metrics are insufficient. Establishing clinically oriented benchmarks—such as SurgVeo and the Surgical Plausibility Pyramid (SPP) that assess tool manipulation validity, tissue response forces, and surgical intent—is an urgent priority. Furthermore, quantifying model uncertainty to indicate prediction confidence and ensuring interpretability to explain failure modes are strictly mandatory in high-stakes healthcare settings.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Evolving Beyond Simulators into Brains
sections.summary: Concluding the survey, we reaffirm the significance of surgical video generation shifting from visual mimicry to causal world models, and summarize the future outlook.
sections.details:
Between 2024 and 2026, surgical video generation progressed from asking "can we generate?" (unconditional) to "can we steer?" (conditional), and now toward "can we predict physical laws and scene causality?" (world models).

Currently, world modeling approaches remain in their infancy, and the transition from pure diffusion models to true world models is still underway. However, when clinical domain knowledge, rigorous biomechanics, and trusted clinical evaluation metrics converge, surgical video generation will evolve far beyond a realistic video synthesizer—serving as a powerful virtual digital twin for training and validating next-generation surgical robots.

takeaways: Surgical video generation is shifting its core purpose: moving from competing on visual realism to acting as world models that predict causal dynamics and state changes driven by robot actions.

Standard pixel-level metrics like FVD and FID fail to detect anatomical and physical violations (clinical implausibility), creating an urgent need for domain-specific evaluation benchmarks like SurgVeo.

To produce physically plausible videos, combining diffusion models with biomechanical priors or symbolic physics engines (e.g., SWoMo) represents a promising breakthrough over standalone diffusion models.
limitations: World-modeling surgical video generation is still in its early stages with very few implementations (e.g., SWoMo), and direct demonstrations of successful robotic policy learning remain to be proven.
Datasets are heavily biased toward specific surgical procedures and single institutions, leaving zero-shot generalization across different endoscopic hardware and surgical sites largely unverified.
